title: The Research Process
bigQuestion: When eight sources all claim to answer your question, how do you decide which ones deserve your trust?

story.title: Eight Sources, Three Survivors
story.kicker: A student types a question into a search bar, gets eight promising results, and then does the hard part: asking each one to prove itself.
paragraphs: Marisol's question was simple to say and hard to answer: what really started the Great Chicago Fire of 1871? She had heard the story about Mrs. O'Leary's cow kicking over a lantern. Her uncle swore it was true. Her history teacher said nobody knows. Marisol wanted to find out for herself, so on a Tuesday night she opened a laptop and typed the question in. The screen filled with results in less than a second. She picked the first eight that looked useful and pasted their links into a document.

Then she went back and looked at each one slowly. Source one was a blog post with no author's name and no date, and it repeated the cow story as fact. Source two was a page selling Chicago tours; the fire was a paragraph between two ads. Source three was a video with dramatic music and a narrator who never said where his facts came from. Source four was a student essay someone had posted online. Marisol crossed all four out. Not one could tell her who wrote it, when, or why she should believe it.

Source five was a newspaper article from 1871, scanned and posted by a library. It was written days after the fire, by a reporter who was there. Source six was a book by a historian, published by a university press, with notes showing where every fact came from. Source seven was the website of the Chicago History Museum, which had a page on the fire's causes. These three could answer her hard questions. She kept them.

Source eight was the interesting one. It was a 1893 newspaper piece in which a reporter admitted he had helped invent the cow story to sell papers. Marisol was not sure at first whether to trust it. Then she found that the historian's book discussed the same confession. Two sources, independent of each other, pointed the same way. That is when a fact starts to feel solid.

Marisol's paper did not say the cow was innocent, because nobody can prove that either. It said the cow story was never proven, that the official inquiry in 1871 could not name a cause, and that a reporter later admitted helping to spread the tale. Every sentence pointed back to a source a reader could check. That is what research is: not collecting claims, but testing them, and then showing your work.
story.think: Marisol threw out four sources in five minutes. What questions did she ask that let her decide so fast, and which of those questions could you ask about any source?

lessons.title: Narrowing a Topic to a Question
lessons.mainIdea: A topic is a subject; a research question is a specific thing you want to find out, and only the question can guide a search.
reading: A student says, "My paper is about social media." That is a *topic*, and it is the size of an ocean. You cannot research an ocean. You can research one wave. A *research question* is a question about the topic that is narrow enough to answer and open enough to be worth answering. "Does social media use affect how well high school students sleep?" is a wave. It names who, what and which effect. It could be answered with evidence.

To narrow a topic, add limits. Limit the group: not everyone, but teenagers in the United States. Limit the time: not all of history, but the last ten years. Limit the angle: not every effect, but sleep, or grades, or friendship. Then turn the narrowed topic into a question that starts with how, why, to what extent, or does. A good question cannot be answered with a single word you already know. "Is social media popular?" is not worth ten pages. "Why did one Chicago high school ban phones, and what changed?" might be.

Test your question before you commit to it. Is it too big? If you could write a book on it, cut it down. Is it too small? If one sentence on a museum website answers it, open it up. Is it actually a question, or a claim you already believe? "Why is social media bad for teens?" has decided the answer before the research begins. "How does social media use relate to teen sleep?" leaves room for the evidence to surprise you. Good researchers want to be surprised. That is the whole reason to look.

words.d: the general subject an essay or research project is about
a specific, answerable question that guides a search for evidence
how much a question or project covers; its size

look.title: Four Questions, One Topic
look.text: Topic: the Chicago River. Question A: What is the Chicago River? Question B: Why did engineers reverse the flow of the Chicago River in 1900, and did it work? Question C: Is the Chicago River good? Question D: What is the history of every river in Illinois?
look.prompt: Which question has the right scope for a five-page paper, and what is wrong with each of the other three?

check.q: What is the difference between a topic and a research question?
choices: A topic is a broad subject; a research question is a specific, answerable question about it
A topic is a question; a research question is the answer
A topic is always about history; a research question is always about science
There is no difference; the terms mean the same thing
check.why: A topic like social media is a subject; a research question narrows it to something specific you can actually find out.

check.q: Which question would the lesson call too small?
choices: How has the Chicago River changed since 1900?
What year was the Chicago River reversed?
Why do cities build canals?
To what extent did the river reversal improve public health?
check.why: A single date can be found in one sentence on a museum website; it does not need a paper.

check.q: Why is "Why is social media bad for teens?" a weak research question?
choices: It is about a topic that is too old
It uses the word teens
It has already decided the answer before any evidence is found
It is too short to be a question
check.why: The question assumes social media is bad, so it leaves no room for the evidence to surprise the researcher.

lessons.title: Searching Like a Researcher
lessons.mainIdea: Good searching means choosing precise keywords, using search tools on purpose, and knowing when to leave the open web for a library database.
reading: Typing your whole question into a search box works badly. The search engine matches words, not meanings, so "why did the Chicago River get reversed" pulls in every page with the word river. Researchers search with *keywords*, the two or four words that carry the meaning. For that question, the keywords are Chicago River reversal 1900. Add a word to narrow, drop a word to widen. If results are about the wrong thing, add a minus sign before the word you want gone: reversal -car keeps out pages about backing up a vehicle.

Quotation marks tell a search engine to find an exact phrase. Searching "Sanitary and Ship Canal" with the marks finds pages that use that exact name. Without the marks you get pages about canals, ships and sanitation separately. Search engines also let you limit results by date or by site. Adding site:.gov shows only government pages; adding site:.edu shows only college and university pages. These are not always the best pages, but they are a fast way to find sources with a name behind them.

For serious work, the open web is only the first stop. A *database* is a searchable collection of published articles, books and records that a library pays for. Illinois students can search many databases free through their school library or through the state's online library service. The articles there were edited and checked before they were published, which the open web does not promise. A good research day often goes like this: search the web to learn the vocabulary of your topic, then take that vocabulary into a database to find the sources you will actually cite.

words.d: a word or short phrase that carries the main meaning of a search
an organized, searchable collection of published sources, usually provided by a library
a symbol or word, like quotation marks or a minus sign, that tells a search engine how to search

look.title: Same Question, Fewer Words
rows: why did the chicago river get reversed and did it work
look.prompt: The last search is not the shortest, yet it would probably give the most useful results. What do its extra words do that the first search's extra words do not?

check.q: What do quotation marks do in a search?
choices: They make the search find only videos
They tell the search engine to find that exact phrase
They remove that word from the results
They limit results to the last year
check.why: Marks around a phrase ask for pages that contain those words together in that order.

check.q: Why does the lesson suggest going to a library database after searching the web?
choices: Databases are faster than search engines
Databases contain only sources about Illinois
Database sources were edited and checked before publication, which the open web does not promise
Databases do not require keywords
check.why: A database holds published, edited material, so its sources are more likely to hold up.

check.q: A search for Chicago River reversal keeps returning pages about cars. What should the researcher add?
choices: More words about rivers
The word please
Quotation marks around the whole question
A minus sign before car, as in -car
check.why: The minus sign tells the engine to leave out pages containing that word.

lessons.title: Authority and Accuracy
lessons.mainIdea: Ask who is behind a source and whether its claims can be checked; a source that hides its author or its evidence has not earned your trust.
reading: The first question to ask a source is who wrote it, and why should I believe that person? This is the source's *authority*. A historian who spent ten years in the Chicago archives has authority on the fire. A tour company does not, even if its page is well written. Authority is not the same as fame. A famous actor has no special authority on medicine. Look for an author's name, the author's job or training, and the organization that published the piece. If you cannot find any of those, the source is asking you to trust a stranger in the dark.

The second question is whether the source is *accurate*: are its facts right, and can I check them? A careful source shows where its information came from, through footnotes, links, a list of works cited, or phrases like "according to the 1871 inquiry." That trail lets you follow a claim back to its origin. A source with no trail may still be right, but you have no way to know. Try this test: pick one specific fact from the source, such as a date or a number, and check it against a second source you already trust. If it fails, the whole source is suspect.

Watch for signs of carelessness. Misspelled names, dates that do not match, and claims that are bigger than the evidence all warn you. So does language that sounds sure about things nobody can be sure of. "Mrs. O'Leary's cow definitely started the fire" should make you suspicious, because the 1871 inquiry could not name a cause. Honest sources say what they know and admit what they do not. A source that admits uncertainty is usually more reliable than one that never does.

words.d: the knowledge, training or position that gives a source the right to be believed on a subject
the quality of being correct and free of errors
to check that something is true by comparing it with other evidence

look.title: Two Pages on the Same Fire
look.text: Page one: no author, no date, bright ads on both sides, and the sentence "Everyone knows the cow did it." Page two: written by a museum curator, dated last year, with a note at the bottom listing the 1871 inquiry transcript and two history books. Page two says, "The cause was never determined."
look.prompt: Page one gives a clear answer and page two does not. Explain why page two is still the more useful source for a research paper.

check.q: Which source has the most authority on the causes of the 1871 fire?
choices: A tour company's web page
A famous actor's post about Chicago
A student's essay posted online
A historian who studied the fire's records for years
check.why: Authority comes from real knowledge and training on the specific subject.

check.q: What is one quick test of a source's accuracy from the lesson?
choices: Check one specific fact against a source you already trust
Count how many ads the page has
See whether the page loads quickly
Ask whether the author is famous
check.why: If a checkable fact turns out wrong, the rest of the source becomes suspect.

check.q: Why does the lesson say a source that admits uncertainty is often more reliable?
choices: Because uncertain sources are shorter
Because honest sources say what they know and admit what they do not
Because all facts are uncertain
Because uncertain sources are always newer
check.why: Overconfidence about unknowable things is a warning sign; honest limits are a sign of care.

lessons.title: Currency and Purpose
lessons.mainIdea: Check when a source was made and why; a date tells you whether the information is still good, and a purpose tells you which way it might lean.
reading: *Currency* means how recent a source is. It matters more for some questions than for others. If your question is about the best treatment for a disease, a source from 1995 may be dangerously out of date. If your question is about what people believed in 1871, a source from 1871 is exactly what you need. Ask: has anything changed since this was written that would change its answer? Look for a publication date, and on web pages look for a "last updated" line. A page with no date at all is hard to judge, which is one reason to prefer pages that have one.

*Purpose* is the reason the source exists. Every source was made by someone who wanted something. A scientist wants to report what an experiment showed. A company wants to sell you a product. A campaign wants your vote. A comedian wants a laugh. None of these purposes makes a source useless, but each one shapes what the source says and leaves out. A page from a bottled water company may have real facts about tap water, but it will choose the facts that make bottled water look good. Knowing the purpose tells you where to push.

You can often find the purpose by asking who pays for the source and who benefits if you believe it. Look at the web address: .gov is a government site, .edu is a school, .org is often but not always a nonprofit, and .com is usually a business. Read the About page. Notice whether the source gives both sides of a question or only one. *Bias* is a lean toward one side, and every writer has some. The problem is hidden bias, the kind that pretends to be neutral. A source that says up front what it wants is easier to use honestly than one that hides it.

words.d: how recent or up to date a source is
the reason a source was created, such as to inform, persuade, sell or entertain
a lean toward one side of a question that shapes what a source includes and leaves out

look.title: How Old Is Too Old?
rows: Reporter's confession about the cow story
look.cite: years of the sources in this chapter's opening story
look.prompt: The oldest source here is also one of the most valuable. For which kinds of research questions is an old source a strength, and for which is it a weakness?

check.q: For which question would a source from 1871 be a strength rather than a weakness?
choices: What is the safest way to treat a burn today?
What did Chicagoans believe about the fire right after it happened?
How many people live in Chicago now?
Which smartphone has the best camera?
check.why: A source from the time is exactly what you need to learn what people believed then.

check.q: A bottled water company's page has facts about tap water. What does knowing the purpose tell a researcher?
choices: The facts are all false
The page cannot be cited under any circumstances
The page will choose facts that favor bottled water, so check what it leaves out
The page must be recent
check.why: Purpose shapes what a source includes; a seller picks facts that help the sale.

check.q: According to the lesson, which kind of bias is the real problem?
choices: Bias in old sources
Bias in government sources
Bias that a writer states openly
Hidden bias that pretends to be neutral
check.why: Every writer leans somewhere; the danger is a lean disguised as balance.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source comes from the time or the person you are studying; a secondary source studies primary sources, and a strong paper uses both.
reading: Frederick Douglass wrote his Narrative in 1845. He was there. He had been enslaved in Maryland and escaped. When he wrote, "You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man," that sentence is evidence straight from the person who lived it. That is a *primary source*: a record made by someone who took part in or witnessed the events, or an original object from the time. Letters, diaries, speeches, photographs, interviews, lab data, court transcripts and newspaper reports from the day are all primary sources.

A historian's book about Douglass, written in 2010, is a *secondary source*. It studies the primary sources, compares them, and builds an interpretation. Secondary sources are enormously useful. They give you context you would need years to gather yourself, and they tell you what experts have concluded. But they are one step removed. Every secondary source chose which primary sources to look at and how to read them. Two historians can look at the same letters and tell different stories.

Whether a source is primary or secondary depends on your question. A 1995 book about the Chicago fire is a secondary source if your question is about the fire. It is a primary source if your question is how historians in the 1990s wrote about disasters. A strong research paper uses both kinds. Primary sources let you see for yourself and quote the people who were there. Secondary sources tell you what that evidence has been taken to mean and where the arguments are. If you only have secondary sources, you are reporting other people's conclusions. If you only have primary sources, you may be missing what everyone else already figured out.

words.d: an original record made by a participant or witness, or an object from the time being studied
a work that studies, interprets or summarizes primary sources
an explanation of what evidence means

look.title: A Witness Speaks for Himself
look.text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
look.cite: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845
look.prompt: What can this sentence tell a researcher that a historian's summary of Douglass's life could not, and what could the historian add that the sentence alone cannot?

check.q: Which of these is a primary source for a paper on the 1871 Chicago fire?
choices: A newspaper report written days after the fire
A 1995 history book about the fire
A documentary made in 2015
An encyclopedia entry
check.why: A report from the time, by someone who was there, is an original record of the event.

check.q: Why is a secondary source described as "one step removed"?
choices: Because it is always older than the primary source
Because it studies and interprets primary sources rather than recording events directly
Because it is always shorter
Because it was written by a student
check.why: A secondary source works from the records rather than being one of them.

check.q: A student's paper uses only secondary sources. What is the risk the lesson names?
choices: The paper will be too long
The paper will have too many quotations
The student is only reporting other people's conclusions
The sources will be too old
check.why: Without primary evidence, the writer never sees the record for themselves.

lessons.title: Quote, Paraphrase, Summarize
lessons.mainIdea: Take notes in three modes, quoting exact words, paraphrasing in your own words, or summarizing the whole, and mark which mode each note is in.
reading: Here is a sentence from a museum page: "The fire began on the evening of October 8, 1871, in or near a barn on DeKoven Street, and burned for about two days." There are three ways to take a note on it. A *quotation* copies the exact words inside quotation marks. A *paraphrase* restates the idea in your own words and sentence shape, about the same length: The fire started near a DeKoven Street barn on the night of October 8, 1871, and lasted roughly two days. A *summary* boils a longer passage down to its main point in far fewer words: fire began Oct. 8, 1871, DeKoven St., two days.

Quote when the exact words matter: when the wording is striking, when you plan to analyze it, or when changing it might change the meaning. Paraphrase for most facts and ideas, because your paper should sound like you, not like a string of other people's sentences. Summarize when you need the gist of a whole page or chapter. A common mistake is a paraphrase that only swaps a few words: The fire started on the evening of October 8, 1871, in or close to a barn on DeKoven Street. That is not a paraphrase. It is the source's sentence wearing a hat. A real paraphrase closes the source, writes from memory, then checks the facts.

Mark every note with its mode. Put quotation marks around exact words the moment you copy them. Write P for paraphrase or S for summary at the top of the note. Write the page number on every note, even if you think you will remember. Weeks later, when you draft, those marks are the only way to know which words are yours. Students who get accused of copying are often students who took sloppy notes and forgot what was quoted. Careful notes are the cheapest insurance there is.

words.d: a source's exact words, copied and placed inside quotation marks
a restatement of a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure
a brief statement of a longer passage's main points

look.title: Is This a Paraphrase?
look.text: Source: "By 1900 Chicago's population had passed 1.6 million, making it the second largest city in the country." Note A: By 1900 Chicago's population had gone past 1.6 million, making it the second biggest city in the nation. Note B: Chicago grew so fast that by 1900 more than 1.6 million people lived there; only one American city was larger.
look.prompt: Which note is a true paraphrase and which is the source's sentence with a few words swapped? What did the better note change?

check.q: When should a researcher quote instead of paraphrase?
choices: Whenever the source is long
When the source is a website
When the note is about a date
When the exact wording matters or will be analyzed
check.why: Quotation preserves wording that is striking or that the paper will examine closely.

check.q: What makes a note "the source's sentence wearing a hat"?
choices: Swapping a few words but keeping the source's sentence shape
Copying the words with quotation marks
Summarizing a whole chapter in one line
Adding a page number
check.why: A true paraphrase changes both the words and the structure; a light word swap is still copying.

check.q: Why does the lesson say to write the page number on every note?
choices: Because teachers require it
Because without it you cannot cite or recheck the fact later
Because page numbers show authority
Because notes without numbers are too short
check.why: Weeks later, the page number is the only way back to the exact spot in the source.

lessons.title: The Source Log
lessons.mainIdea: Record every source's full details the moment you find it, in one place, so that nothing you use is ever lost or uncitable.
reading: Every researcher has lived this moment: the paper is due tomorrow, there is a perfect fact in the draft, and nobody remembers where it came from. The fix is boring and it works. A *source log* is a single list, on paper or in a file, where you record every source the moment you decide it might be useful. For each one, write the author, the full title, the publisher or website, the date, the page numbers you used, and the web address if there is one. Give each source a number or a short label, such as Museum or Smith 1995.

Then use that label on every note. A note that reads Smith 1995, p. 42, P: inquiry could not name a cause tells you three things at a glance: which source, which page, and that the words are your own paraphrase. When you draft, you pull the label into the sentence as a citation. When you build your works cited list, the log already has everything you need, in one place, and you do not have to go hunting through browser history at midnight.

The log also records your judgment. Add a line for each source saying what it is good for and what its limits are: strong on dates, weak on causes; written to sell tours; the only primary source I have on the inquiry. This turns your log into a map of your evidence. You can see at a glance if all your sources lean the same way, if you have no primary sources, or if one source is doing all the work. Those are the problems best caught early, while there is still time to search again.

words.d: a running list of every source found, with the details needed to cite it
a note in a paper that tells the reader exactly which source a fact or quotation came from
a short name or number given to a source so notes can refer to it quickly

look.title: Where the Notes Came From
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a model source log
look.prompt: One source produced half the notes. What is the risk of that pattern, and what would you look for in the log before deciding whether it is a problem?

check.q: What belongs in a source log entry?
choices: Only the web address
Only the author's name
Author, title, publisher, date, pages used and address
The whole text of the source
check.why: The log holds everything a citation and works cited entry will need.

check.q: What does the note "Smith 1995, p. 42, P" tell the researcher?
choices: The source, the page, and that the note is a paraphrase
That the source is a primary source
That the note is a quotation
That the source was published on page 42
check.why: The label names the source, the page number locates the fact, and P marks the mode.

check.q: Why should the log include a line about each source's strengths and limits?
choices: To make the log longer
To help catch problems like all sources leaning one way
Because citations require it
To replace the works cited list
check.why: Judgment notes turn the log into a map that shows gaps and imbalances early.

lessons.title: Synthesis, Not Stacking
lessons.mainIdea: Synthesis puts sources in conversation around your own idea; stacking just lines them up one after another with no thinking between them.
reading: Read this paragraph from a first draft. Smith says the fire's cause was never proven. The museum says the cause is unknown. The 1871 newspaper blamed the cow. A reporter later admitted he made the cow story up. That is four sources, one after another, like cans on a shelf. It is *stacking*. Every sentence is true and cited, and the paragraph still says nothing, because the writer never appears. There is no idea holding the cans together.

Now read it again after revision. The cow story spread within days of the fire, appearing in the newspaper before the official inquiry had even begun, yet the inquiry could not name any cause, and both Smith and the Chicago History Museum treat the cause as unknown. The story's staying power came less from evidence than from how good it was as a story, which a reporter admitted in 1893 when he confessed to helping invent it. The same four sources are there. But now the writer has a point, that the cow story outran the evidence, and the sources are arranged to support it. That is *synthesis*: combining sources to build an idea that none of them states alone.

To synthesize, look for the relationships between your sources. Where do they agree? That agreement is strong evidence. Where do they disagree? That disagreement is often your most interesting paragraph. Does one source explain something another only mentions? Does a primary source show what a secondary source claims? Write those relationships down before you draft. Then write sentences that start with your idea and bring the sources in to support it, instead of sentences that start with a source's name. A paper that says "Smith says" at the start of every sentence is a book report. A paper that says "The evidence points two ways" is research.

words.d: combining ideas from several sources to build a new point that none of them states alone
listing sources one after another without connecting them or adding an idea
the way two sources connect: agreeing, disagreeing, explaining or supporting

look.title: Three Sources on Phones in Class
look.text: Source A, a survey: 62 percent of students say phones distract them in class. Source B, a teacher's essay: a phone ban raised participation in her classes. Source C, a student newspaper: many students use phones for translation and reading support. A draft paragraph says: A says phones distract. B says the ban helped. C says students need phones.
look.prompt: Rewrite the draft's idea in one sentence that puts the three sources in conversation. What relationship between B and C does your sentence have to deal with?

check.q: What is wrong with a paragraph that stacks sources?
choices: The facts are usually false
It has too few citations
It is always too long
The writer's own idea never appears to connect them
check.why: Stacking lists sources without the idea that would hold them together.

check.q: In the revised paragraph, what idea holds the four sources together?
choices: The cow story spread faster than the evidence supported
The cow definitely started the fire
Newspapers in 1871 were always accurate
The inquiry proved the reporter lied
check.why: The writer's point, that the story outran the evidence, arranges the sources into an argument.

check.q: According to the lesson, which kind of sentence marks synthesis rather than stacking?
choices: A sentence that begins with a source's name
A sentence that begins with the writer's idea and brings sources in to support it
A sentence with no citation
A sentence that quotes two sources in a row
check.why: When the idea leads and the sources follow, the writer is thinking with the sources rather than listing them.

lessons.title: What Plagiarism Is
lessons.mainIdea: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, on purpose or by accident, and the cure is careful notes and clear credit.
reading: *Plagiarism* is using another person's words or ideas without giving them credit, so that a reader thinks they are yours. The word comes from a Latin word for kidnapper. Copying a paragraph from a website is plagiarism. So is copying a sentence and changing three words. So is taking a source's idea, stating it in your own words, and not saying where it came from. So is turning in a paper someone else wrote, or that a program wrote for you. The rule is about honesty, not about words alone.

Most student plagiarism is not a plan to cheat. It is an accident born of bad notes. A student copies a sentence into a notes file without quotation marks, forgets a month later that it was copied, and pastes it into the draft as her own. The reader cannot tell the difference between that accident and theft, and the consequences at most schools are the same. That is why the earlier lessons insisted on marking every note. Some students also plagiarize out of fear: they do not trust their own sentences, so they borrow better ones. Your own clear sentence, with credit, always beats a borrowed one.

What does not need a citation? *Common knowledge*: facts that any reader could find in many general sources, such as Chicago being in Illinois or the fire happening in 1871. Your own ideas, observations and arguments need no citation either. Everything else does: exact words, specific facts and numbers, and other people's interpretations, even in your own words. When you are unsure, cite. No teacher has ever lowered a grade for a citation that was not strictly needed. Many have failed papers for one that was missing.

words.d: presenting another person's words or ideas as your own without giving credit
widely known facts that can be found in many general sources and need no citation
acknowledgment of the source of words or ideas

look.title: Which Ones Need a Citation?
look.text: 1. Chicago sits on the shore of Lake Michigan. 2. About 300 people died in the 1871 fire, according to one historian's estimate. 3. The idea that the cow story lasted because it was a good story, which a student thought of after reading Smith's book. 4. The claim, from Smith's book, that the inquiry was rushed. 5. "The city was a furnace," from an 1871 letter.
look.prompt: Sort the five into needs a citation and does not. For each one that needs it, say whether the writer should quote, paraphrase or simply cite the idea.

check.q: Which of these is plagiarism?
choices: Quoting a source with quotation marks and a citation
Stating that Chicago is in Illinois without a citation
Restating a source's interpretation in your own words with no citation
Citing your own observation
check.why: An idea taken from a source needs credit even when the words are yours.

check.q: What does the lesson say causes most student plagiarism?
choices: A plan to cheat
Sloppy notes that lose track of what was copied
Teachers who assign too much
Using library databases
check.why: Copied sentences without marks turn into accidental plagiarism weeks later.

check.q: Which fact is common knowledge and needs no citation?
choices: A historian's estimate of the number of dead
A reporter's confession about the cow story
The claim that the inquiry was rushed
The fact that the fire happened in 1871
check.why: The year of the fire appears in countless general sources; an estimate or a specific claim does not.

lessons.title: MLA In-Text Citations
lessons.mainIdea: In MLA style, a short note in parentheses, usually the author's last name and a page number, points the reader to the full entry in the works cited list.
reading: *MLA* stands for the Modern Language Association, a group of teachers of English and languages that publishes a style guide most high school English classes follow. Its system for giving credit has two parts that work together. In the body of the paper, a short *in-text citation* points to a source. At the end, the *works cited* list gives the full details. The in-text part is small on purpose, so it does not interrupt the reading. Its job is only to say which source and where.

The basic form is the author's last name and the page number in parentheses, with no comma between them and no p.: The inquiry could not settle on a cause (Smith 42). The period comes after the closing parenthesis. If you name the author in your sentence, leave the name out of the parentheses: Smith notes that the inquiry could not settle on a cause (42). If a source has no page numbers, such as a web page, give only the author: (Chicago History Museum). If there is no author, use a shortened form of the title in quotation marks or italics, whichever the works cited entry uses: ("Great Fire").

Quotations follow the same rules. Put the citation after the closing quotation mark and before the period: One witness wrote that "the city was a furnace" (Jones 3). Two authors get both names: (Lee and Park 17). Three or more get the first name and et al., a Latin phrase meaning and others: (Lee et al. 17). Every in-text citation must match the first word of an entry in the works cited list. That match is the whole point: a reader sees (Smith 42), turns to the list, finds Smith, and can go check page 42.

words.d: the Modern Language Association, whose style guide sets rules for citing sources in English classes
a short note in parentheses within the paper that identifies the source of a fact or quotation
a Latin abbreviation meaning and others, used for three or more authors

look.title: Three Sentences, Three Forms
look.text: The inquiry could not settle on a cause (Smith 42). Smith notes that the inquiry could not settle on a cause (42). The museum's page states plainly that the cause "was never determined" (Chicago History Museum).
look.cite: model sentences written for this lesson
look.prompt: Explain why each citation looks different. What would change in the first sentence if Smith's book had two authors?

check.q: What is the basic form of an MLA in-text citation for a book?
choices: (Smith 42)
(Smith, p. 42)
(page 42, Smith)
check.why: MLA uses the author's last name and page number, no comma, no p.

check.q: Where does the citation go in a sentence that ends with a quotation?
choices: Before the quotation begins
Inside the quotation marks
After the period
After the closing quotation mark and before the period
check.why: The parentheses sit between the closing quotation mark and the sentence's final period.

check.q: Why must an in-text citation match the first word of a works cited entry?
choices: So the paper is alphabetical
So a reader can find the full source in the list and check it
So the citation is shorter
Because et al. requires it
check.why: The short note is a pointer; it only works if it leads to the right full entry.

lessons.title: The Works Cited List
lessons.mainIdea: A works cited list gives full details for every source cited, in alphabetical order, so a reader can find each one.
reading: The *works cited* list is the last page of an MLA paper. It is titled Works Cited, centered, and it includes every source you cited in the paper and nothing you did not. Entries are in alphabetical order by the first word, usually the author's last name. Each entry uses a *hanging indent*: the first line starts at the left margin and every line after it is indented. The list is double-spaced like the rest of the paper. The purpose is simple. Anyone who reads your paper should be able to find every source you used.

MLA builds each entry from the same set of pieces in the same order, using only the pieces that apply. Author. Title of the source. Title of the larger container it sits in, such as a website, a journal or a collection. Other contributors. Version. Number. Publisher. Date. Location, such as page numbers or a web address. A book by one author needs only a few of these: Smith, Karen. The Fire and the City. University of Illinois Press, 1995. A web page needs others: "The Great Chicago Fire." Chicago History Museum, 2023, www.chicagohistory.org/great-fire. Titles of whole works, like books and websites, are italicized. Titles of parts, like articles and web pages, go in quotation marks.

A magazine or journal article shows the container idea clearly: Lee, Ana. "Rumor and Fire." Journal of Urban History, vol. 22, no. 3, 2019, pp. 40-58. The article is the source; the journal is its container; the volume, issue, year and pages locate it. When a piece has no author, start with the title and alphabetize by it. When you are unsure of a format, look it up rather than guess; the MLA publishes examples, and most school libraries have the handbook. What matters most is not perfect commas but completeness: every source a reader would need, with enough detail to find it.

words.d: the alphabetical list at the end of an MLA paper giving full details for every source cited
a format in which the first line of an entry sits at the margin and later lines are indented
the larger work a source sits inside, such as a journal, website or book of essays

look.title: Three Entries
look.text: Smith, Karen. The Fire and the City. University of Illinois Press, 1995. // Lee, Ana. "Rumor and Fire." Journal of Urban History, vol. 22, no. 3, 2019, pp. 40-58. // "The Great Chicago Fire." Chicago History Museum, 2023, www.chicagohistory.org/great-fire.
look.cite: model entries written for this lesson (the sources are invented)
look.prompt: Put the three entries in the order they would appear on a works cited page, and explain which pieces each entry has that the others lack.

check.q: How are entries in a works cited list ordered?
choices: In the order they were cited
Alphabetically by the first word, usually the author's last name
By date, newest first
By type: books, then articles, then websites
check.why: Alphabetical order lets a reader find an entry from the in-text citation's first word.

check.q: Which title would be italicized in MLA style?
choices: An article in a journal
A web page on a museum site
A book
A chapter in a book
check.why: Whole works, like books and journals, are italicized; parts of them go in quotation marks.

check.q: In the entry for "Rumor and Fire," what is the container?
choices: Ana Lee
The page numbers
The year 2019
The Journal of Urban History
check.why: The article sits inside the journal, which is its container.

lessons.title: The Annotated Bibliography
lessons.mainIdea: An annotated bibliography adds a short paragraph under each citation that summarizes the source and judges how useful it is.
reading: An *annotated bibliography* is a works cited list with a paragraph under each entry. That paragraph is the *annotation*. It usually does three things in about four to six sentences. It summarizes what the source says. It evaluates the source: who wrote it, how reliable it is, what its purpose and limits are. And it explains how the source will help your project. Teachers often assign one before the paper itself, because writing it forces you to actually read your sources and think about them instead of collecting links.

Here is a model annotation for an invented source. Smith, Karen. The Fire and the City. University of Illinois Press, 1995. Smith traces the fire from the first alarm through the rebuilding, using the 1871 inquiry transcripts and dozens of letters. She argues that the cow story survived because it gave a frightened city someone to blame. Smith is a professional historian, and her notes let a reader check every claim, though the book is now nearly thirty years old. This will be my main secondary source on the fire's causes and the inquiry.

Notice what the annotation does not do. It does not praise the source in vague words like great or interesting. It does not just repeat the title. It names the evidence the source uses, states its argument in one sentence, gives a real reason to trust it and a real limit, and says exactly what job it will do. Write your annotations from your source log; the judgment lines you wrote there are the seeds. A good annotated bibliography is your research in miniature. Read it straight through and you should be able to see the shape of the paper you are about to write.

words.d: a list of sources in citation form, each followed by a short paragraph of summary and evaluation
the paragraph under a citation that summarizes and judges the source
to judge the quality, reliability and usefulness of something

look.title: Fix This Annotation
look.text: Entry: "The Great Chicago Fire." Chicago History Museum, 2023. Annotation: This is a great website about the Chicago fire. It has a lot of interesting information and pictures. I found it really useful and I will use it in my paper.
look.prompt: This annotation breaks every rule in the lesson. Rewrite it in four sentences that summarize, evaluate and explain the source's job, inventing reasonable details.

check.q: What three things does a good annotation do?
choices: Summarize, evaluate, and explain how the source will be used
Quote, paraphrase, and summarize
List the author, title, and date
Praise, criticize, and recommend
check.why: An annotation reports what the source says, judges it, and states its job in the project.

check.q: Why do teachers often assign an annotated bibliography before the paper?
choices: Because it is shorter than a paper
Because it forces students to actually read and think about their sources
Because it replaces the works cited list
Because it does not require citations
check.why: Writing annotations makes the reading and judging happen before drafting.

check.q: Which sentence belongs in a strong annotation?
choices: This source is really great.
The title is The Fire and the City.
I liked this one a lot.
Smith's notes let a reader check every claim, though the book is nearly thirty years old.
check.why: That sentence gives a specific reason to trust the source and a specific limit.

review.q: A student wants to write about climate change. What should she do first?
choices: Find eight sources
Narrow the topic to a specific, answerable research question
Write the introduction
Build the works cited list
review.why: A topic cannot be researched until it becomes a question with limits on group, time and angle.

review.q: Which search would most likely return the fewest useless results?
choices: why do rivers get reversed
"Chicago River" reversal 1900
river
chicago
review.why: Exact-phrase marks plus specific keywords tell the engine precisely what to find.

review.q: A web page has no author, no date, and ads on every side. Which of the four tests does it fail most clearly?
choices: Currency only
Purpose only
Authority and currency
None; it may be used freely
review.why: No author means no authority; no date means no way to judge currency.

review.q: Which of these is a secondary source for a paper on Frederick Douglass?
choices: Douglass's 1845 Narrative
A letter Douglass wrote
A photograph of Douglass
A 2010 biography of Douglass
review.why: The biography studies primary sources; the Narrative, letter and photo come from Douglass himself.

review.q: A note copies a sentence exactly but has no quotation marks. What is the likely result?
choices: Accidental plagiarism when the sentence lands in the draft as the student's own
A stronger paper
A shorter works cited list
Nothing; notes do not need marks
review.why: Without marks, the writer forgets the words were copied and presents them as her own.

review.q: What is the difference between synthesis and stacking?
choices: Synthesis uses more sources
Synthesis uses only primary sources
Synthesis connects sources around the writer's own idea; stacking lists them
Stacking is used in MLA and synthesis in other styles
review.why: Synthesis puts sources in conversation to build a point; stacking just lines them up.

review.q: Which in-text citation is correct MLA form for a quotation from page 17 of a book by Lee and Park?
choices: (Lee and Park, p. 17)
(Lee & Park 17)
(Lee, Park, 17)
(Lee and Park 17)
review.why: MLA joins two authors with and, then gives the page with no comma or p.

review.q: What does a works cited entry for a journal article include that a book entry does not?
choices: The container's title, volume, issue and page range
The author's name
The year
A hanging indent
review.why: An article sits inside a journal, so the entry must name that container and locate the article in it.
